title: Research Bite #36: Students ignore their mistakes
author: Craig Barton
summary: Research Bite #36 summarizes Uwe Maier and Christian Klotz's study of how secondary students engage with elaborated error feedback inside a digital German grammar learning system, drawing on more than 20,000 formative assessment cases from 2,826 students across 182 classrooms in grades 5 to 11. The central finding is that students with low prior knowledge — precisely the group who would benefit most from detailed error explanations — are the least likely to seek, comprehend, or value that feedback, while higher-achieving students engage with it more readily, creating a 'Matthew effect' that can widen knowledge gaps over time. Task complexity compounds the problem: as courses get harder, students may seek feedback slightly more often but review it less thoroughly, likely due to cognitive load or feelings of being overwhelmed. Barton's takeaway for teachers is that assigning feedback is not the same as students using it: monitoring feedback-seeking behavior, not just performance scores, is needed to catch disengagement. The paper argues for actively scaffolding low-knowledge students' feedback literacy rather than assuming struggling students will naturally gravitate toward the help that's available to them.
points: Students with low prior knowledge are least likely to seek out, comprehend, or value elaborated error feedback — even though they are the group who stands to benefit from it the most, a pattern the authors call a “Matthew effect.”
Across 20,000+ real assessment cases in a digital learning system, feedback engagement tracked prior achievement more strongly than the quality or availability of the feedback itself.
As task complexity rises, students may click into feedback slightly more often but review it less deeply — a sign of cognitive overload rather than genuine engagement.
Performance scores alone hide this problem: teachers need visibility into whether students are actually seeking, reading, and using feedback, not just whether they got questions right or wrong.
quotes: This scholarly article explores how secondary school students interact with error feedback in a digital German grammar learning application.

The study analyzed over 20,000 assessment cases from a real-world educational setting, revealing that prior knowledge significantly impacts feedback engagement, with higher-achieving students being more likely to seek and appreciate feedback.
Students with low prior knowledge are less likely to seek and engage with elaborated error feedback, despite being the group who could benefit from it the most.

While these students could benefit the most from such detailed feedback to close knowledge gaps, they are paradoxically less likely to seek, comprehend, and perceive its usefulness, often ignoring it entirely.

Low formative assessment scores, indicating low prior knowledge, are strongly associated with reduced error feedback seeking and error feedback comprehension, as well as a more critical perspective on error feedback usefulness.
Teachers should monitor student engagement and provide targeted support to help them utilize feedback effectively.
